To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the introduction of a fear-inducing stimulus (a loud bell) into the situation of the mother-surrogate relationship resulted in the development of an avoidance pattern of behavior in which the monkey would avoid the surrogate when the bell was ringing and approach the surrogate when it had ceased to ring.

the presence of a mild aversive stimulus (a buzzer) during the development of affectional responses in rhesus monkeys results in (1) a decrease in the time spent with the surrogate, and (2) a decrease in responsiveness to the surrogate when the surrogate is presented in the absence of the buzzer.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the introduction of a secondary drive, based upon fear, upon the approach-withdrawal response pattern to a positive drive stimulus.
the effect of a conflict situation on the development of the attachment behavior of the rhesus infant.
the effects of an aversive shock stimulus upon the development of the rhesus monkey’s affectional responsiveness to the artificial mother surrogate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the aversive stimulus was associated with a decrease in the amount of contact with the surrogate and an increase in the amount of locomotion.

the introduction of the aversive situation during the early development of the infant monkey's response to the surrogate results in a significant reduction in the total amount of contact with the surrogate and a concomitant increase in the time spent by the monkey in the avoidance position.
the approach-avoidance conflict in the mother-surrogate situation is a function of the relative intensity of the aversiveness associated with the surrogate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a strong positive response to the surrogate is not necessarily an unconditioned response to the surrogate, but rather a response to an aversive stimulus.
in the mother-surrogate situation, the introduction of a fear stimulus into the locus of positive reward results in a marked decrease in the amount of time spent in contact.
a strong aversive stimulus, such as shock, when presented in the context of the mother-surrogate situation, produces a significant decrease in contact time with the surrogate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the approach-avoidance conflict model of the development of anxiety is an important one to consider.
the aversive stimulus associated in the mother-surrogate situation is not the same as that associated with food and water.
the aversive stimulus, in this case, the presentation of a loud noise, can be used effectively to reduce the time spent in the proximity of the mother surrogate.
